title: Name the video's visual philosophy before drawing any shot
when: Planning the look of a whole video, before the first scene or picture is designed.
summary: Great visual work starts from a stated point of view, not from a layout. Name the video's look in a few words (a 'movement'), say in one paragraph how it lives in space, colour, scale, rhythm and hierarchy, then let every shot express it.
steps: Give the look a short name of one or two words that a designer would recognise as a stance (for example 'quiet ledger' or 'stone and fire').
Write how it shows in form and space, in colour and material, in scale and rhythm, and in what draws the eye first.
Check each scene against it: a shot that could belong to any video gets changed until it belongs to this one.
avoid: Starting from a stock layout and decorating it.
A philosophy that repeats the script's topic instead of describing how things look.
checks: The video's direction names its look in a few words and one paragraph.
Every scene can be traced back to that look.
source: anthropics/skills canvas-design (Apache-2.0), pinned 2c5958e: design philosophy first, then expression; restated for drawn and designed video shots.

title: On the second pass, refine what is there instead of adding more
when: Reviewing or polishing a storyboard, a picture or a designed shot that is already planned.
summary: When a shot feels weak the instinct is to add another prop, effect or word. The stronger move is to make the existing elements more coherent: better placement, scale, spacing, timing and colour relationships.
do: Before adding an element, ask how the elements already there could do the job better.
Tighten spacing and alignment so nothing touches or overlaps by accident.
Cut an element that competes with the focal point rather than adding a second focal point.
avoid: Fixing a flat shot with a filter, a sparkle or an extra caption.
Adding a new idea in the review pass.
checks: The polish pass removed or adjusted more than it added.
source: anthropics/skills canvas-design (Apache-2.0), pinned 2c5958e: the final refinement step; restated.

title: Spot the generic defaults and spend the freedom on choices made for this video
when: Choosing staging, symbols, palettes and moves for any shot that is not fixed by the style or the script.
summary: AI-made visuals cluster around the same defaults. They are not wrong, but they are what any similar video would get. Where the owner's style or the script leaves a choice free, do not spend it on a default: make a choice that only fits this story.
do: Before drawing, list the default you would reach for (a lone figure in the centre with a question mark, a light bulb for an idea, money raining for money, a clock for time, a globe for 'the world', the same slow push on every shot, a title above three icons) and replace it with something from this story's world.
Prefer the story's own objects, places and gestures over universal symbols.
Keep a default only when the brief asks for it, and say so in the notes.
avoid: Universal symbols where the words name something concrete.
The same camera move or transition repeated through a section.
checks: No scene uses a stock symbol where the script names a specific thing.
Camera moves and compositions vary within each section.
source: anthropics/skills frontend-design (Apache-2.0), pinned 2c5958e: calibration against the traits generated design clusters around; restated for storyboards.

title: Plan the design system, review it against the brief, build, then critique
when: Designing the colours, type and layout rules of a video before its scenes are drawn.
summary: Write a small design system first (4-6 named colours with hex values, one or two typefaces with roles, a layout idea, a few principles). Read it back against the brief and change whatever would fit any similar video. Only then build, and critique the result while building.
steps: Write the palette as 4-6 named hex colours with their roles.
Name the typefaces and what each is for.
Describe the layout idea in one sentence per scene type.
Review the plan: change every part that reads as a default rather than a choice for this brief, and note what changed.
Build, then look at the result and fix what does not match the plan.
avoid: Building first and finding a system afterwards.
checks: The design plan names its palette, type roles and layout idea before any shot is designed.
source: anthropics/skills frontend-design (Apache-2.0), pinned 2c5958e: two passes, plan reviewed against the brief before building; restated.

title: Spend boldness in one place per shot; keep the rest quiet
when: Composing any shot that has more than one element.
summary: A shot reads when one element is clearly the memorable thing. Let that element be big, bright or moving; keep everything around it disciplined and subordinate.
do: Decide the one element that carries the shot and give it the size, contrast or motion.
Keep supporting elements smaller, calmer and closer to the background colour.
Cut decoration that does not serve the line being spoken.
avoid: Several elements competing in size, colour and motion at once.
checks: Each shot has one clear focal element.
source: anthropics/skills frontend-design (Apache-2.0), pinned 2c5958e: restraint and self-critique; restated.

title: Open on the most characteristic thing of the subject's world
when: Designing the first shot of the video or of a new chapter.
summary: The first thing the viewer sees should be the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in its strongest form: an object, a place, a moment in motion. A generic title card or a big number with a small label is the default; use it only when it truly is the strongest picture.
do: Name the single most characteristic image of this topic and open on it.
Make the first frame a finished composition, never a half-entered element.
avoid: Opening on a generic title card, a logo or an empty background.
checks: The hook shot shows something only this topic would show.
source: anthropics/skills frontend-design (Apache-2.0), pinned 2c5958e: ground the design in the subject matter; restated for video hooks.

title: Numbers, labels and dividers only when they carry information
when: Adding on-screen labels, counters, numbered markers, rules or chips.
summary: Structure is information. Numbered markers belong to real sequences (steps, rankings, a timeline); labels belong to things the viewer would otherwise not identify. Decorative structure makes a video look templated.
do: Use 1-2-3 markers only for real steps or rankings.
Label only what the picture cannot make obvious.
avoid: A label that repeats what the picture already shows.
Numbered chips on items that are not a sequence.
checks: Every label and number on screen tells the viewer something new.
source: anthropics/skills frontend-design (Apache-2.0), pinned 2c5958e: visual structure is information; restated.

title: One orchestrated reveal lands better than effects everywhere
when: Deciding entrances, effects and motion across a scene.
summary: Motion draws attention, so it is spent where attention is needed. A single well-timed reveal per scene is stronger than every element sliding and fading in the same way.
do: Choose the one moment in the scene that deserves a designed reveal and time it to its word.
Let the other elements arrive simply or be there from the start.
avoid: The same fade-and-rise entrance on every element.
Effects that run when nothing is being said about them.
checks: Each scene has at most one big orchestrated reveal.
source: anthropics/skills frontend-design (Apache-2.0), pinned 2c5958e: motion used sparingly and deliberately; restated for video.

title: Weave the topic in as a quiet reference, not a caption
when: Designing abstract backdrops, patterns, title designs and transitions.
summary: The best designed shots carry the subject in their form: a pattern built from the topic's shapes, a colour taken from its world, a texture that belongs to it. Someone who knows the topic feels it; everyone else just sees a good composition.
do: Build backgrounds and patterns from shapes of the subject's world.
Take accent colours from the story's materials (fire, clay, gold, ocean).
avoid: Explaining the reference with words on screen.
checks: Abstract backdrops and patterns are related to the subject.
source: anthropics/skills canvas-design (Apache-2.0), pinned 2c5958e: deducing the subtle reference; restated.

title: Hold every frame to a master's craftsmanship
when: Before a picture, designed shot or drawing is accepted.
summary: Professional work looks labored over: nothing falls off the frame, nothing overlaps by accident, every element has breathing room and margins, and the colours feel chosen together.
checks: Nothing important touches the frame edge or is cut off.
Every element has clear space around it.
The palette is limited and cohesive.
avoid: Accepting a frame because it is 'nearly' right.
source: anthropics/skills canvas-design (Apache-2.0), pinned 2c5958e: craftsmanship requirements; restated as checks.

title: Use seeded variation so repeated things differ but stay reproducible
when: Drawing crowds, particles, patterns, foliage, stars or any repeated element.
summary: Repeated elements look machine-made when they are identical, and look broken when they change between renders. Vary size, angle, timing and colour from a seed, so every copy differs and the same frame always renders the same.
do: Give each repeated element its own seed-derived size, rotation, delay and colour shift.
Keep the variation inside a narrow range so the group still reads as one thing.
avoid: Unseeded randomness that changes the frame on every render.
checks: Repeated elements vary, and the same frame renders identically twice.
source: anthropics/skills algorithmic-art (Apache-2.0), pinned 2c5958e: seeded randomness and controlled parameters; restated.

title: Choose one named colour theme for the video and keep it
when: Picking the palette and type of a video or a channel.
summary: A palette works best as a named theme with a mood (for example 'ocean depths', 'golden hour', 'forest canopy', 'arctic frost', 'desert rose'): a background, a primary, an accent and one or two neutrals, plus a heading and body typeface. Pick the theme that fits the story and keep it for the whole video.
do: Name the theme and its mood.
List its colours by role: background, ink, accent, support.
Use the accent only where the eye must go.
avoid: Mixing colours from different themes in one video.
checks: The video's design names one theme and every shot uses its colours.
source: anthropics/skills theme-factory (Apache-2.0), pinned 2c5958e: curated themes of colour and type; restated.

title: Write skills that explain why, with examples, not only rigid rules
when: The owner writes or edits a skill in the Skills room.
summary: A skill generalises when it says what it is for and why each rule matters, gives a worked example, and keeps 'always' and 'never' for the few rules that truly are absolute. The 'when' line decides whether the program picks it, so it names the situations plainly.
do: Say in the 'when' line the concrete situations the skill is for.
Give the reason behind each rule.
Add one short example of the rule applied.
avoid: Long lists of capitalised MUST and NEVER rules without reasons.
checks: The skill has a 'when' line naming situations and at least one reason.
source: anthropics/skills skill-creator (Apache-2.0), pinned 2c5958e: writing skills that trigger and generalise; restated for the Skills room.
